subject: Physics
title: The Mystery of the Amber Beads
hook: Anjali discovers why a comb attracts paper scraps after she combs her hair—and learns the law that powers the universe.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student observing electrostatic phenomena in her home lab

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Physics tutor who explains the science behind it

slides.title: Electric Charges and Fields
slides.storyContext: Anjali combs her hair and notices the comb attracts tiny paper scraps. Why?

image.alt: Electric Charges and Fields — Electric Charges and Fields

slides.title: The Comb Experiment
slides.storyContext: Anjali is getting ready for school in Delhi. She combs her hair and spots something magical—the plastic comb now sticks to bits of paper on her study desk, even without touching them. 'Ravi uncle, what magic is this?' she asks her tutor. Ravi smiles. 'Not magic, Anjali—it's electric charge, the fundamental force that holds atoms together and powers lightning storms.'

image.alt: The Comb Experiment — Electric Charges and Fields

slides.title: What is Electric Charge?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Electric charge (q or Q) is a fundamental property of matter. There are two types: positive (protons) and negative (electrons). Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.

points.label: Unit
points.text: Coulomb (C). Elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C. An electron has charge −e; a proton has charge +e.

points.label: Conservation
points.text: Total charge is conserved in an isolated system. Charges cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred.

image.alt: What is Electric Charge? — Electric Charges and Fields

slides.inSimpleWords: Charge is the property that makes things attract or repel each other. It comes in two flavors—positive and negative—and cannot be made or destroyed.

slides.title: Coulomb's Law

points.label: Statement
points.text: The electrostatic force between two point charges q1 and q2 separated by distance r is: F = k q1 q2 / r^2, where k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2 (often approximated 9 × 10^9).

points.label: Key insight
points.text: Force is directly proportional to both charges and inversely proportional to the square of distance. Double the distance? Force drops to one-fourth.

points.label: Vector nature
points.text: Force is along the line joining the charges. Repulsive if charges have the same sign, attractive if opposite signs.

example.problem: Two charges: q1 = 2 × 10^-6 C and q2 = 3 × 10^-6 C, separated by r = 0.1 m. Find the force between them.

slides.inSimpleWords: The force between two charges depends on how strong each charge is and how far apart they are. Closer = stronger force.

image.alt: Coulomb's Law — Electric Charges and Fields

slides.title: Electric Field

points.label: Definition
points.text: Electric field E at a point is the force per unit positive test charge: E = F / q_test, with units N/C or V/m.

points.label: Field from a point charge
points.text: For a point charge Q at distance r: E = k Q / r^2, directed radially outward if Q > 0, inward if Q < 0.

points.label: Superposition
points.text: Net field from multiple charges is the vector sum of individual fields. Fields add like vectors.

image.alt: Electric Field — Electric Charges and Fields

slides.inSimpleWords: The electric field is the influence a charge spreads around itself. It tells you what force a test charge would feel at any point.

slides.title: Field Lines and Gauss's Law

points.label: Field lines
points.text: Imaginary lines showing the direction of E. They start on positive charges and end on negative charges. Density of lines ∝ field strength.

points.label: Gauss's Law
points.text: Total electric flux through a closed surface = Q_enclosed / ε₀, where ε₀ = 8.85 × 10^-12 C^2/(N·m^2). Mathematically: ∮ E·dA = Q_enclosed / ε₀.

points.label: Significance
points.text: Gauss's law is a powerful tool for finding E when charge distribution is symmetric (sphere, cylinder, plate).

slides.inSimpleWords: Field lines are invisible paths showing the direction of the field. Gauss's law lets you count the total field passing through a surface.

image.alt: Field Lines and Gauss's Law — Electric Charges and Fields

slides.title: Conductors vs Insulators

points.label: Conductors
points.text: Metals (copper, aluminum) have free electrons. In electrostatic equilibrium, E = 0 inside, all charge sits on the surface. E is perpendicular to surface.

points.label: Insulators
points.text: Non-metals (rubber, glass) have electrons bound to atoms. E penetrates; charges remain wherever placed.

points.label: Charging by induction
points.text: Bringing a charged object near an uncharged conductor causes charges to separate, creating an induced charge. No actual charge transfer.

slides.inSimpleWords: In metals, charges are free to move and rush to the surface. In rubber or glass, charges stay put.

image.alt: Conductors vs Insulators — Electric Charges and Fields

slides.title: Solved Problem: Three Charges in a Row

example.problem: Three point charges: q1 = +1 μC at x = 0, q2 = −2 μC at x = 0.1 m, q3 = +1 μC at x = 0.2 m. Find the net force on q2.
example.solution: Force on q2 from q1: F₁ = k (1 × 10^-6) (2 × 10^-6) / (0.1)^2 = 1.8 N, pointing right (attractive). Force on q2 from q3: F₃ = k (1 × 10^-6) (2 × 10^-6) / (0.1)^2 = 1.8 N, pointing left (attractive). Net force on q2 = 1.8 − 1.8 = 0 N (the two forces cancel).

slides.inSimpleWords: When a charge sits between two others of opposite sign, the forces can balance completely.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Three Charges in a Row — Electric Charges and Fields

points.text: Anjali rubs a balloon on her dry hair and it sticks to the ceiling. The balloon acquires a negative charge of 5 μC. Assume the ceiling has an induced positive charge of 5 μC over an area of 0.01 m^2. Estimate the average electric field between the balloon and ceiling, assuming they are 0.05 m apart. (Hint: E ≈ σ / ε₀, where σ is surface charge density.)

example.problem: What is the electric field and attractive force?
example.solution: Charge density σ = 5 × 10^-6 / 0.01 = 5 × 10^-4 C/m^2. Electric field E = σ / ε₀ ≈ (5 × 10^-4) / (8.85 × 10^-12) ≈ 5.65 × 10^7 N/C. Force F = qE = (5 × 10^-6) × (5.65 × 10^7) ≈ 0.28 N ≈ 28 grams-force, enough to hold the balloon.

image.alt: Challenge: The Balloon Trick — Electric Charges and Fields

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Electric charge exists in two types—positive and negative—and is conserved.
Coulomb's law: F = k q₁ q₂ / r², the inverse-square law for electrostatic force.
Electric field E = F / q_test measures the field strength; field lines show its direction.
Gauss's law: ∮ E·dA = Q_enclosed / ε₀, a powerful symmetry tool.
In conductors, charges rearrange to make E = 0 inside; in insulators, E penetrates.

slides.inSimpleWords: Charges push and pull via electric fields. The closer or stronger, the bigger the force. Metals hide the field inside; insulators let it through.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Electric Charges and Fields

subject: Physics
title: The Bottled Lightning: Capacitors
hook: Ravi shows Anjali how a capacitor stores electric energy—and why camera flashes need them to survive.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student exploring energy storage in electrical circuits

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Tutor demonstrating capacitor function with a real camera flash

slides.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
slides.storyContext: When Ravi's camera flash fails, Anjali asks why. 'The capacitor is discharged,' he says. 'A capacitor is like a battery that can store and release electrical energy almost instantly.'

image.alt: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: The Camera Flash
slides.storyContext: Anjali is at a wedding in Mumbai. The photographer's flash quits mid-ceremony. Ravi explains: 'The capacitor inside the flash stores electrical energy when the camera is idle. When you press the shutter, the capacitor releases all that energy at once, creating a bright pulse of light. Without capacitors, we couldn't have instant, bright flashes.'

image.alt: The Camera Flash — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: Electric Potential

points.label: Definition
points.text: Electric potential V at a point is the work per unit positive charge to bring a test charge from infinity to that point: V = W / q, with units volts (V) = J/C.

points.label: Potential from a point charge
points.text: For a point charge Q: V = k Q / r. The potential is a scalar (not a vector). Reference point is at infinity (V = 0).

points.label: Potential difference
points.text: Voltage U_AB = V_A − V_B. This is the work per unit charge to move a charge from B to A.

image.alt: Electric Potential — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.inSimpleWords: Potential is the 'height' of the electric field. Higher potential means more energy per charge. Moving against the field (uphill) costs work; moving downhill releases energy.

slides.title: Equipotentials and Relationship to E

points.label: Equipotential surfaces
points.text: Surfaces where V is constant. No work is needed to move a charge along an equipotential. E is always perpendicular to equipotential surfaces.

points.label: E and V relationship
points.text: Electric field is the negative gradient of potential: E = −dV/dr (in 1D). In other words, E points in the direction of steepest V decrease.

points.label: Uniform field
points.text: Between two parallel plates separated by distance d at potentials V_A and V_B: E = |V_A − V_B| / d.

slides.inSimpleWords: Field lines are perpendicular to equipotentials. The field points downhill (from high to low potential).

image.alt: Equipotentials and Relationship to E — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: What is a Capacitor?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A capacitor is two conductors separated by an insulator. When charged, one plate holds +Q, the other −Q. Potential difference U appears between them.

points.label: Capacitance C
points.text: Defined as C = Q / U, with units farads (F) = C/V. Higher C means the capacitor stores more charge for the same voltage.

points.label: Parallel plate capacitor
points.text: For two square plates of area A, separated by distance d with permittivity ε₀: C = ε₀ A / d. Larger area or smaller gap ⟹ larger capacitance.

example.problem: A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area A = 0.01 m^2 and separation d = 0.001 m. Find its capacitance. (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10^-12 F/m)

slides.inSimpleWords: A capacitor is an electrical container. Its capacitance tells you how much charge it holds for each volt applied.

image.alt: What is a Capacitor? — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: Energy Stored in a Capacitor

points.label: Energy formula
points.text: Energy U = (1/2) C V^2 = (1/2) Q V = (1/2) Q^2 / C. Measured in joules (J). The energy is stored in the electric field between the plates.

points.label: Energy density
points.text: Energy per unit volume in the field: u = (1/2) ε₀ E^2. For a parallel plate capacitor with field E = V/d, this gives U = (1/2) ε₀ E^2 × (A × d) = (1/2) ε₀ A V^2 / d.

points.label: Camera flash example
points.text: A tiny capacitor charged to 300 V with C = 100 μF stores U = (1/2) × 100 × 10^-6 × (300)^2 ≈ 4.5 J—enough to power a bright flash.

slides.inSimpleWords: The more you charge a capacitor (higher Q or V), the more energy it stores. That's why camera flashes are dangerous—they hold a punch!

image.alt: Energy Stored in a Capacitor — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: Capacitors in Series and Parallel

points.label: Parallel connection
points.text: Capacitors share the same voltage U. Total capacitance: C_total = C_1 + C_2 + C_3 + … (capacitances add). Larger total capacitance.

points.label: Series connection
points.text: Capacitors share the same charge Q. Voltage divides. Reciprocals add: 1/C_total = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 + 1/C_3 + … Smaller total capacitance.

points.label: Analogy
points.text: Parallel is like adding tanks to a system—more storage. Series is like adding resistances—reduces flow.

example.problem: Two capacitors: C_1 = 2 μF and C_2 = 3 μF. Find total C in series and in parallel.
example.solution: Parallel: C_total = 2 + 3 = 5 μF. Series: 1/C_total = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, so C_total = 6/5 = 1.2 μF.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel capacitors act like bigger containers (C adds). Series capacitors act like a narrower pipe (1/C adds).

image.alt: Capacitors in Series and Parallel — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: Dielectrics in Capacitors

points.label: Dielectric constant κ
points.text: When an insulator (dielectric) is placed between plates, the capacitance increases: C_dielectric = κ C_vacuum, where κ > 1 (e.g., κ = 2 for paper, κ = 80 for water).

points.label: Mechanism
points.text: The dielectric's molecules polarize in response to the field, creating an internal field that opposes the applied field, allowing more charge to accumulate.

points.label: Practical use
points.text: Dielectrics increase capacitance without changing plate area or separation. They also allow higher voltages before breakdown.

slides.inSimpleWords: Filling the gap with plastic, paper, or ceramic instead of air makes a capacitor store more charge—like packing more into the same container.

image.alt: Dielectrics in Capacitors — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: Solved Problem: Charging and Discharging

example.problem: A 10 μF capacitor is charged to 100 V, then connected across a 50 Ω resistor. How much energy is released? How long until it drops to 1 V?
example.solution: Initial energy U_i = (1/2) × 10 × 10^-6 × (100)^2 = 0.05 J. Energy released = 0.05 J. Discharge follows V(t) = V_0 e^(-t/RC), where RC = 50 × 10 × 10^-6 = 5 × 10^-4 s. Time to 1 V: 1 = 100 e^(-t/RC), so e^(-t/RC) = 0.01, giving t = RC × ln(100) ≈ 5 × 10^-4 × 4.6 ≈ 2.3 × 10^-3 s = 2.3 ms.

slides.inSimpleWords: When a capacitor discharges through a resistor, the voltage drops exponentially. A bigger capacitor or resistor means slower discharge.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Charging and Discharging — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

points.text: A portable defibrillator must deliver 200 J of energy in one shock. The capacitor is charged to 4000 V. What capacitance C is needed? (Use U = (1/2) C V^2)

example.problem: Solve for C.

image.alt: Challenge: Designing a Defibrillator Capacitor — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Electric potential V is work per unit charge; voltage is the potential difference U_AB = V_A − V_B.
Electric field E = −dV/dr is perpendicular to equipotential surfaces.
Capacitance C = Q / U measures charge storage; for parallel plates, C = ε₀ A / d.
Energy U = (1/2) C V^2 is stored in the electric field.
In parallel, C_total = C_1 + C_2; in series, 1/C_total = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2.
Dielectrics increase C by factor κ; they also allow higher voltages.

slides.inSimpleWords: Capacitors are electrical batteries that store energy in an electric field, release it instantly, and power flashy things like camera flashes and defibrillators.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

subject: Physics
title: Lights, Fans, and Ohm's Law
hook: Why does a 60 W bulb glow brighter than a 40 W bulb? Anjali rewires her desk lamp and discovers the science of electrical power.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student experimenting with home electrical circuits

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Tutor explaining Ohm's law and circuit analysis

slides.title: Current Electricity
slides.storyContext: Anjali plugs in two light bulbs and wonders: why is one brighter? Ravi says, 'It's all about current, resistance, and power.'

image.alt: Current Electricity — Current Electricity

slides.title: The Brightness Mystery
slides.storyContext: At her study desk in Bangalore, Anjali notices two identical 230 V lamps—one rated 60 W, the other 40 W. Both glow when plugged into the same outlet, but the 60 W lamp is visibly brighter. 'Why,' she asks Ravi, 'does one bulb burn brighter if they get the same voltage?' Ravi smiles. 'Because the bright one uses more current—and current, resistance, and power are the keys to understanding electricity.'

image.alt: The Brightness Mystery — Current Electricity

slides.title: Electric Current and Charge Flow

points.label: Current definition
points.text: Electric current I is the rate of charge flow: I = Q / t, measured in amperes (A) = coulombs per second (C/s). 1 A = 1 C/s.

points.label: Direction convention
points.text: Conventional current direction is the flow of positive charges (opposite to electron flow). Current flows from + to − through external circuits.

points.label: Current density
points.text: Current per unit area: J = I / A, measured in A/m^2. For a wire with cross-section A carrying current I, J = I/A.

image.alt: Electric Current and Charge Flow — Current Electricity

slides.inSimpleWords: Current is the flow of electrical charge. It's measured in amps—how many coulombs per second are moving through a wire.

slides.title: Ohm's Law and Resistance

points.label: Ohm's Law
points.text: Voltage V across a conductor is proportional to current I through it: V = I R, where R is resistance (ohms, Ω). Rearranged: I = V/R and R = V/I.

points.label: Resistance formula
points.text: For a wire: R = ρ L / A, where ρ is resistivity (Ω·m), L is length, and A is cross-sectional area. Longer wires have higher R; thicker wires have lower R.

points.label: Temperature dependence
points.text: Resistivity increases with temperature: ρ(T) = ρ_0 [1 + α(T − T_0)], where α is the temperature coefficient (∼ 0.004 K^-1 for copper).

example.problem: A copper wire has resistivity ρ = 1.7 × 10^-8 Ω·m, length L = 10 m, and cross-section A = 1 mm^2 = 10^-6 m^2. Find its resistance.

slides.inSimpleWords: Resistance is the wire's opposition to current flow. Longer or thinner wires resist more. Ohm's law ties voltage, current, and resistance together: V = IR.

image.alt: Ohm's Law and Resistance — Current Electricity

slides.title: Resistors in Series and Parallel

points.label: Series
points.text: Resistors in series: same current through all, voltage divides. Total resistance R_total = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + … (resistances add).

points.label: Parallel
points.text: Resistors in parallel: same voltage across all, current divides. Reciprocals add: 1/R_total = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3 + …

points.label: Power in series vs parallel
points.text: In series, total power P = I^2 R_total splits among resistors: P_i = I^2 R_i. In parallel, resistors with lower R dissipate more power.

example.problem: Two resistors: R_1 = 10 Ω, R_2 = 20 Ω. Voltage across both = 30 V. Find total current and power if connected (a) in series, (b) in parallel.

slides.inSimpleWords: Series resistors block more (R adds). Parallel resistors reduce R (easier path). Parallel draws more current and dissipates more power.

image.alt: Resistors in Series and Parallel — Current Electricity

slides.title: Electrical Power and Energy

points.label: Power formula
points.text: Power P = V I (watts, W). Also P = I^2 R = V^2 / R. 1 watt = 1 joule/second.

points.label: Energy
points.text: Energy consumed over time t: E = P t (joules). Home meters measure kilowatt-hours (kWh): 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10^6 J.

points.label: Heat dissipation
points.text: In a resistor, electrical energy converts to heat: Q = I^2 R t. This is why wires heat up when current flows.

slides.inSimpleWords: Power is how fast energy is used. Higher voltage or current means more power. Energy = power × time, measured in kWh for your home bill.

image.alt: Electrical Power and Energy — Current Electricity

slides.title: Electromotive Force and Internal Resistance

points.label: EMF (ε)
points.text: Electromotive force is the non-conservative force that drives current around a circuit. It's not actually a force—it's energy per unit charge, measured in volts.

points.label: Internal resistance r
points.text: Real batteries have internal resistance r. Terminal voltage V = ε − I r (ε is EMF, r is internal resistance).

points.label: Circuit equation
points.text: For a battery ε, internal resistance r, external resistance R: I = ε / (R + r), and terminal voltage V = ε − I r.

example.problem: A 12 V battery with internal resistance r = 0.5 Ω is connected to an external load R = 11.5 Ω. Find current and terminal voltage.

slides.inSimpleWords: A battery's EMF is the energy it gives per coulomb of charge. But inside, resistance drops some voltage, so the terminal voltage is less.

image.alt: Electromotive Force and Internal Resistance — Current Electricity

slides.title: Solved Problem: Bulb Brightness Revisited

example.problem: A 60 W bulb and a 40 W bulb are both rated 230 V. Find the resistance of each. When both are plugged into 230 V mains, which dissipates more current?
example.solution: P = V^2 / R, so R = V^2 / P. For 60 W: R_60 = (230)^2 / 60 = 52900 / 60 ≈ 881.67 Ω. For 40 W: R_40 = (230)^2 / 40 = 52900 / 40 = 1322.5 Ω. The 60 W bulb has lower resistance. Current through 60 W: I = 230 / 881.67 ≈ 0.26 A. Current through 40 W: I = 230 / 1322.5 ≈ 0.17 A. The 60 W bulb draws more current, so it's brighter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Higher wattage means lower resistance. Lower resistance means more current flows, making the bulb hotter and brighter.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Bulb Brightness Revisited — Current Electricity

points.text: Anjali's home uses: 5 bulbs × 60 W each = 300 W (8 hours/day), 1 refrigerator 500 W (24 hours/day), and 1 geyser 2000 W (1 hour/day). Monthly electricity cost is 8 rupees per kWh. What is the monthly bill? (Assume 30 days.)

example.problem: Calculate total energy and cost.
example.solution: Bulbs: 0.3 kW × 8 × 30 = 72 kWh. Refrigerator: 0.5 kW × 24 × 30 = 360 kWh. Geyser: 2 kW × 1 × 30 = 60 kWh. Total = 72 + 360 + 60 = 492 kWh. Cost = 492 × 8 = Rs 3,936.

image.alt: Challenge: Energy Bill Calculation — Current Electricity

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Current I = Q/t (amps) is the rate of charge flow. Ohm's law: V = IR.
Resistance R = ρL/A depends on material, length, and cross-section.
Series: R_total = ΣR (same current); Parallel: 1/R_total = Σ(1/R) (same voltage).
Power P = VI = I^2 R = V^2/R; Energy E = Pt (kWh for homes).
EMF ε drives current; terminal voltage V = ε − Ir accounts for internal resistance.
Higher wattage bulbs have lower resistance and draw more current—that's why they glow brighter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electricity flows as current through resistances, carrying power. Ohm's law and series/parallel rules let you analyze any circuit.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Current Electricity

subject: Physics
title: Compass Needles and Cosmic Rays
hook: What makes a compass needle point north? Anjali discovers how moving charges create magnetic fields—and how the Earth is a giant magnet.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student investigating magnetism with household materials

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Tutor explaining Lorentz force and magnetic field geometry

slides.title: Moving Charges and Magnetism
slides.storyContext: Anjali plays with a compass and a wire carrying current. Ravi shows her that moving charges create magnetic fields—just like the Earth does.

image.alt: Moving Charges and Magnetism — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.title: The Compass Deflection
slides.storyContext: In her home lab in Kolkata, Anjali sets a compass needle on her desk, pointing north. She holds a wire carrying electric current over the needle. To her amazement, the needle deflects! 'Why does a wire move the compass?' she asks. Ravi explains: 'Every moving charge creates a magnetic field. The Earth is magnetic because of currents deep in its iron core. Your wire's current field deflects the compass needle.'

image.alt: The Compass Deflection — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.title: Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge

points.label: Lorentz force
points.text: A charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B experiences force F = q v × B (vector cross product). Magnitude: F = q v B sin(θ), where θ is angle between v and B.

points.label: Direction
points.text: Use right-hand rule: fingers point along v, curl toward B, thumb points along F. For negative charge, reverse.

points.label: Unit
points.text: Magnetic field B is measured in tesla (T) = kg/(A·s^2). 1 tesla is strong (Earth's field ≈ 50 μT).

image.alt: Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.inSimpleWords: A moving charge in a magnetic field feels a sideways push—perpendicular to both its motion and the field.

slides.title: Circular Motion in a Magnetic Field

points.label: Perpendicular motion
points.text: When v ⊥ B, the magnetic force provides centripetal acceleration. Charge moves in a circle with radius r = m v / (q B).

points.label: Cyclotron frequency
points.text: Angular frequency ω = q B / m (rad/s). Period T = 2π / ω = 2πm / (qB). Frequency f = 1/T = qB / (2πm).

points.label: Application: Mass spectrometry
points.text: Ions of different mass-to-charge ratios (m/q) follow different radii in the same B field. This separates isotopes and identifies molecules.

example.problem: An electron (m = 9.1 × 10^-31 kg, q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C) moves perpendicular to B = 0.1 T at v = 10^6 m/s. Find radius and period.

slides.inSimpleWords: A charged particle in a perpendicular magnetic field spirals in circles—the smaller the charge-to-mass ratio, the bigger the circle.

image.alt: Circular Motion in a Magnetic Field — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.title: Magnetic Field from a Current-Carrying Wire

points.label: Biot-Savart Law (qualitative)
points.text: A current-carrying segment creates a magnetic field. Field circles around the wire (right-hand rule: thumb along current, fingers curl in B direction).

points.label: Long straight wire
points.text: Magnetic field at distance r from wire: B = μ₀ I / (2π r), where μ₀ = 4π × 10^-7 T·m/A (permeability of free space).

points.label: Circular loop
points.text: At the center of a loop of radius a carrying current I: B = μ₀ I / (2a). Field direction given by right-hand rule.

image.alt: Magnetic Field from a Current-Carrying Wire — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.inSimpleWords: Current creates circular magnetic fields. The closer to the wire, the stronger the field. Bigger current or tighter loop means stronger field.

slides.title: Force Between Two Current-Carrying Wires

points.label: Ampère's force law
points.text: Two parallel wires carrying currents I₁ and I₂ separated by distance d experience force per unit length: F/L = μ₀ I₁ I₂ / (2π d).

points.label: Same direction = attraction
points.text: Currents in same direction attract; opposite currents repel.

points.label: Ampere (unit definition)
points.text: The ampere is defined so that two parallel wires 1 m apart, each carrying 1 A, experience a force of 2 × 10^-7 N per meter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wires with current push or pull each other magnetically. Same-direction currents attract like friends; opposite currents repel like enemies.

image.alt: Force Between Two Current-Carrying Wires — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.title: Solenoid and Magnetic Dipole

points.label: Solenoid
points.text: A coil of wire wound around a cylinder. Inside, magnetic field B ≈ μ₀ n I, where n = N/L is turns per unit length, I is current.

points.label: Magnetic dipole moment
points.text: For a current loop: μ = N I A, where N is number of turns, A is loop area. Dipole moment is a vector pointing out via right-hand rule.

points.label: Torque in external field
points.text: A magnetic dipole in field B experiences torque τ = μ × B. Magnitude τ = μ B sin(θ). Dipole aligns with field (lowest energy).

example.problem: A solenoid has N = 1000 turns, length L = 0.2 m, and carries I = 2 A. Find field inside.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wrap wire in a coil and current flows through it: you make a solenoid, a tiny electromagnet. More turns or more current = stronger field.

image.alt: Solenoid and Magnetic Dipole — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.title: Solved Problem: Magnetic Deflection in a CRT

example.problem: In a cathode-ray tube (old TV), an electron (v = 10^7 m/s) enters a uniform magnetic field B = 0.01 T perpendicular to velocity. The deflection region is 0.05 m long. Find deflection angle.
example.solution: Radius of curvature r = mv/(qB) = (9.1 × 10^-31 × 10^7) / (1.6 × 10^-19 × 0.01) ≈ 0.057 m. Arc length in field s = 0.05 m. Deflection angle θ = s/r = 0.05/0.057 ≈ 0.88 rad ≈ 50 degrees.

slides.inSimpleWords: A beam of electrons or other charged particles bends in a magnetic field, like light bending in a lens. Stronger field or slower particles bend more sharply.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Magnetic Deflection in a CRT — Moving Charges and Magnetism

points.text: Earth's magnetic field strength at the equator is approximately 30 μT. A compass needle (magnetic dipole moment μ = 0.1 A·m^2) aligns with the field. What torque does the field exert on the needle if it's tilted 45° from north?

example.problem: Calculate the torque.

image.alt: Challenge: Earth's Magnetic Field — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Lorentz force F = qv × B acts perpendicular to both velocity and magnetic field.
Charged particles in perpendicular B fields move in circles with radius r = mv/(qB).
Current-carrying wires create circular magnetic fields: B = μ₀I/(2πr) for straight wire, B = μ₀I/(2a) at center of loop.
Parallel wires with same-direction currents attract; opposite currents repel.
A solenoid's field B = μ₀nI depends on turn density and current.
Magnetic dipoles (like compass needles) experience torque in external fields and align to lowest energy.

slides.inSimpleWords: Moving charges create magnetic fields, and magnetic fields push moving charges sideways. This powers motors, compasses, and all electromagnetic devices.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Moving Charges and Magnetism

subject: Physics
title: Iron Filings and Permanent Magnets
hook: Why is iron magnetic when iron atoms are neutral? Anjali learns how atomic currents and spin create permanent magnets.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student experimenting with magnets and magnetic materials

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Tutor explaining atomic magnetism and magnetic domains

slides.title: Magnetism and Matter
slides.storyContext: Iron filings arrange in lines around a magnet. Ravi tells Anjali: 'Inside every iron atom, electrons spin like tiny planets, creating invisible magnetic fields.'

image.alt: Magnetism and Matter — Magnetism and Matter

slides.title: The Iron Filing Pattern
slides.storyContext: Anjali sprinkles iron filings on paper above a bar magnet. They arrange in beautiful curved lines. 'The fields are invisible,' Ravi explains, 'but iron is ferromagnetic—its atoms have unpaired electrons that spin, creating tiny magnetic dipoles. When billions align, they make a strong magnet.'

image.alt: The Iron Filing Pattern — Magnetism and Matter

slides.title: Atomic Magnetism

points.label: Bohr magneton
points.text: The fundamental unit of atomic magnetic moment: μ_B = e ℏ / (2 m_e) ≈ 9.27 × 10^-24 J/T, where e is electron charge, ℏ is reduced Planck's constant.

points.label: Orbital and spin magnetism
points.text: Electrons create magnetic moments two ways: (1) orbital angular momentum L, giving μ_L = −(e/2m_e) L; (2) intrinsic spin S, giving μ_S = −(e/m_e) S ≈ −2 μ_B (g-factor ≈ 2).

points.label: Net moment per atom
points.text: Total atomic dipole moment μ = μ_L + μ_S. For closed shells (like noble gases), L = S = 0, so μ = 0. Unpaired electrons give non-zero μ.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electrons spin like tops and orbit like planets, each motion creating a tiny magnet. Many electrons spinning together add up to strong magnetism.

image.alt: Atomic Magnetism — Magnetism and Matter

slides.title: Magnetization and Magnetic Field

points.label: Magnetization M
points.text: Magnetization is magnetic dipole moment per unit volume: M = Σμ / V, with units A/m. Total magnetic dipole moment of a sample: μ_sample = M × V.

points.label: Magnetic field B and auxiliary field H
points.text: In matter: B = μ₀ (H + M) = μ₀ μ_r H, where μ_r is relative permeability. In free space: B = μ₀ H.

points.label: Susceptibility χ
points.text: Magnetization is proportional to applied field: M = χ H, where χ is magnetic susceptibility (dimensionless). So B = μ₀ (1 + χ) H = μ₀ μ_r H.

image.alt: Magnetization and Magnetic Field — Magnetism and Matter

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetization M is how magnetized a material is per unit volume. The internal field B depends on both the applied field and the magnetization.

slides.title: Ferromagnetism and Magnetic Domains

points.label: Ferromagnetism
points.text: In iron, cobalt, nickel: unpaired d-electrons create strong atomic moments. Exchange interaction causes parallel alignment even without external field.

points.label: Magnetic domains
points.text: Ferromagnetic materials consist of regions (domains) where atomic moments are aligned. Each domain acts like a tiny magnet. Unmagnetized material has random domain orientations; net M = 0.

points.label: Hysteresis
points.text: When external field is applied, domains align gradually. When field is removed, domains don't fully return—creating permanent magnetization (remanence). Heating above Curie temperature (1043 K for iron) destroys ferromagnetism.

image.alt: Ferromagnetism and Magnetic Domains — Magnetism and Matter

slides.inSimpleWords: Ferromagnetic materials have regions (domains) where atomic spins align. Applying a field rotates domains toward the field; some stay aligned, creating permanent magnets.

slides.title: Paramagnetism and Diamagnetism

points.label: Paramagnetism
points.text: Materials with unpaired electrons (O₂, many transition metals, rare earths). Atomic moments have no preferred direction, but external field weakly aligns them. Susceptibility χ ≈ 10^-3 to 10^-5, temperature-dependent (Curie law: χ ∝ 1/T).

points.label: Diamagnetism
points.text: All materials have some diamagnetism (even copper, water). External field induces opposite-direction moments in electron orbits (Lenz's law). Susceptibility χ ≈ −10^-5 to −10^-6, temperature-independent. Opposed by stronger paramagnetism or ferromagnetism if present.

points.label: Superconductors
points.text: Perfect diamagnets below critical temperature: χ = −1, completely expel external B field (Meissner effect). Levitating magnets over superconductors are a classic demo.

slides.inSimpleWords: Paramagnetic materials are weakly attracted to magnetic fields. Diamagnetic materials are very weakly repelled. Superconductors are perfect diamagnets.

image.alt: Paramagnetism and Diamagnetism — Magnetism and Matter

slides.title: Hysteresis and Energy Loss

points.label: Hysteresis loop
points.text: Plot B vs H: increasing H increases B (curve bends up); at peak H, B saturates. Decreasing H, B doesn't retrace the same path—lag is hysteresis. At H = 0, remanent field B_r remains (permanent magnet).

points.label: Energy loss
points.text: Area enclosed by hysteresis loop = energy dissipated per cycle per unit volume. For AC-driven ferromagnetic cores (transformers, motors), this is core loss, converted to heat.

points.label: Soft vs hard magnetic materials
points.text: Soft iron: narrow hysteresis loop, easy to magnetize/demagnetize (transformer cores). Hard steel: wide loop, high remanence, hard to change (permanent magnets).

image.alt: Hysteresis and Energy Loss — Magnetism and Matter

slides.inSimpleWords: Hysteresis is the lag when magnetic field is switched. Energy is wasted flipping domains—reason transformers and motors get hot.

slides.title: Earth's Magnetism and Geomagnetism

points.label: Magnetic poles
points.text: Earth's magnetic dipole moment is ~7.9 × 10^15 A·m^2. Magnetic north pole is currently near geographic north pole (but off by ~11°, drifting slowly). South magnetic pole is in Antarctica.

points.label: Magnetic declination and inclination
points.text: Declination = angle between true north and magnetic north (varies by location, ~5° in India currently). Inclination (dip) = angle of B field below horizontal (∼45° in India).

points.label: Origin: liquid iron core
points.text: Slow convection of molten iron in Earth's outer core creates circulating currents, generating a dipole field via dynamo effect. Field reverses every ~200,000 years.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth's iron core circulates like a coil of current, making our planet a giant magnet. Compass needles align with this field, pointing roughly north.

image.alt: Earth's Magnetism and Geomagnetism — Magnetism and Matter

slides.title: Solved Problem: Magnetization of Iron

example.problem: A sample of iron (volume V = 10 cm^3 = 10^-5 m^3) has relative permeability μ_r = 1000 in an applied field H = 1000 A/m. Find magnetization M and total field B.
example.solution: Susceptibility χ = μ_r − 1 = 999. Magnetization M = χ H = 999 × 1000 = 9.99 × 10^5 A/m. Field B = μ₀ μ_r H = (4π × 10^-7) × 1000 × 1000 = 4π × 10^-1 ≈ 1.26 T.

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply a field to iron: magnetization is huge (factor of 1000) compared to vacuum. That's why iron cores strengthen electromagnets.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Magnetization of Iron — Magnetism and Matter

points.text: Iron loses ferromagnetism above its Curie temperature (1043 K). Why? A hint: thermal vibrations randomize atomic dipole orientations, competing with exchange interaction. Above T_C, entropy wins and ferromagnetism vanishes. Show that χ ≈ C/T (Curie law) for paramagnetism, where C is a material constant.

example.problem: Write Curie law and explain why heating destroys ferromagnetism.
example.solution: χ = C/T means susceptibility drops as T increases. Thermal energy ~kT random-orients spins faster than exchange interaction can align them. When kT_C ≈ exchange energy, order collapses and the material becomes paramagnetic. Below T_C, exchange is strong; above T_C, entropy dominates.

image.alt: Challenge: Curie Temperature — Magnetism and Matter

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Atomic magnetism arises from electron orbital motion and spin; basic unit is Bohr magneton μ_B ≈ 9.27 × 10^-24 J/T.
Ferromagnetism (iron, cobalt, nickel): strong unpaired-electron moments with exchange interaction aligning them.
Magnetic domains: regions of aligned dipoles. Unmagnetized material has random domains; applied field rotates them, leaving remanence (permanent magnetism).
Hysteresis: lag between B and H, energy loss proportional to loop area.
Paramagnetism: weak alignment of existing dipoles (χ > 0). Diamagnetism: induced opposite moments (χ < 0).
Earth's magnetic field from circulating currents in liquid iron core; field reverses every ~200,000 years.

slides.inSimpleWords: Materials become magnets when atomic spins align. Ferromagnets have permanent alignment; others weakly align or repel. Heating destroys alignment by shaking atoms randomly.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Magnetism and Matter

subject: Physics
title: Faraday's Discovery: Making Power from Magnetism
hook: A changing magnetic field can generate electricity without a battery. Anjali swings a magnet near a coil and watches a meter jump.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student discovering electromagnetic induction with a coil and magnet

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Tutor explaining Faraday's law and Lenz's law

slides.title: Electromagnetic Induction
slides.storyContext: Anjali swings a bar magnet toward a coil connected to an ammeter. Mysteriously, the meter needle deflects—without any battery!

image.alt: Electromagnetic Induction — Electromagnetic Induction

slides.title: The Swinging Magnet
slides.storyContext: In her physics lab in Mumbai, Anjali holds a bar magnet near a coil wired to an ammeter. When she swings the magnet toward the coil, the meter jumps—current flows! When she holds the magnet still, the current stops. 'Ravi uncle, how can a magnet make electricity?' she asks. Ravi smiles: 'Faraday discovered that a *changing* magnetic field induces an electric field. This is the secret behind generators, transformers, and all AC power.'

image.alt: The Swinging Magnet — Electromagnetic Induction

slides.title: Magnetic Flux

points.label: Flux definition
points.text: Magnetic flux Φ (or Φ_B) is the magnetic field passing through a surface: Φ = ∫ B · dA. For uniform field perpendicular to area A: Φ = B A. Unit: weber (Wb) = tesla·m^2 (T·m^2).

points.label: Flux through a coil
points.text: For a coil with N turns, area A, in uniform field B at angle θ to normal: Φ = N B A cos(θ). Maximum when B is perpendicular to coil (θ = 0); zero when B is parallel to coil plane (θ = 90°).

points.label: Changing flux
points.text: Time-varying flux Φ(t) is key to induction. The rate of change dΦ/dt drives induced EMF.

image.alt: Magnetic Flux — Electromagnetic Induction

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic flux is how much field is threading through a surface. More field or bigger area means more flux. Angling the field reduces flux (cos effect).

slides.title: Faraday's Law

points.label: The law
points.text: Induced EMF in a circuit equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux: ε = −dΦ/dt. For N-turn coil: ε = −N dΦ/dt.

points.label: Negative sign (Lenz's law)
points.text: Negative sign means induced EMF opposes the change. If flux increases, induced EMF creates current to oppose it (pushes field out); if flux decreases, induced current tries to preserve it (pulls field in).

points.label: Motional EMF interpretation
points.text: When a conductor moves through B, charges experience Lorentz force F = qv × B, creating separation of charge and EMF = B L v (L is conductor length perpendicular to both v and B).

example.problem: A coil has N = 100 turns, area A = 0.02 m^2, and is in a uniform field B = 0.5 T. The field is perpendicular to the coil and decreases uniformly from 0.5 T to 0 T in Δt = 0.1 s. Find induced EMF.
example.solution: Initial flux Φ_i = N B A = 100 × 0.5 × 0.02 = 1 Wb. Final flux Φ_f = 0. Change ΔΦ = Φ_f − Φ_i = −1 Wb. Rate dΦ/dt = ΔΦ/Δt = −1/0.1 = −10 Wb/s. Induced EMF ε = −dΦ/dt = −(−10) = 10 V.

slides.inSimpleWords: Faraday's law: changing magnetic flux generates electric voltage. Faster change means higher voltage. Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change.

image.alt: Faraday's Law — Electromagnetic Induction

slides.title: Motional EMF and Generators

points.label: Rod moving through field
points.text: When a rod of length L moves perpendicular to B with velocity v: EMF = B L v. This is the principle of mechanical generators.

points.label: Rotating coil (AC generator)
points.text: A rectangular coil rotates in uniform B field. Flux Φ(t) = NBA cos(ωt) (N turns, B field strength, A area, ω angular frequency). Induced EMF ε(t) = NBA ω sin(ωt) = ε₀ sin(ωt), where ε₀ = NBA ω is peak EMF.

points.label: Frequency relation
points.text: For N coil rotations per second, frequency f = N_rot (Hz). Angular frequency ω = 2πf. Peak EMF ε₀ = NBA ω = NBA × 2πf.

image.alt: Motional EMF and Generators — Electromagnetic Induction

slides.inSimpleWords: Spinning a coil in a magnetic field generates alternating voltage. Faster spin or stronger field means higher peak voltage. This is how power plants make electricity.

slides.title: Self-Inductance and Mutual Inductance

points.label: Self-inductance L
points.text: When current I in a coil changes, it creates changing flux through itself, inducing a back-EMF: ε_self = −L (dI/dt), where L is self-inductance (henries, H). L = N Φ / I for a coil.

points.label: Mutual inductance M
points.text: Primary coil with current I₁ creates flux through secondary coil. Secondary EMF ε₂ = −M (dI₁/dt). Similarly, ε₁ = −M (dI₂/dt). Mutual inductance M₁₂ = M₂₁.

points.label: Inductor energy
points.text: Energy stored in inductor: U = (1/2) L I^2. Analogous to capacitor's U = (1/2) C V^2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inductance is the 'reluctance' to change current. Changing current in a coil induces a back-EMF that opposes the change (Lenz's law).

image.alt: Self-Inductance and Mutual Inductance — Electromagnetic Induction

slides.title: Transformers

points.label: Transformer principle
points.text: Primary coil (N_p turns) carries changing current I_p, creating flux Φ. Secondary coil (N_s turns) links the same flux. Induced EMF ratio ε_s / ε_p = N_s / N_p (ideal transformer).

points.label: Voltage and current relations
points.text: V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p. Power is conserved (ideal): V_p I_p = V_s I_s, so I_s / I_p = N_p / N_s (inverse ratio).

points.label: Step-up and step-down
points.text: If N_s > N_p: voltage increases, current decreases (step-up transformer). If N_s < N_p: voltage decreases, current increases (step-down transformer). Power lines use step-up (13 kV → 400 kV) to reduce loss; homes use step-down (230 V).

example.problem: A transformer steps down 230 V to 12 V. Primary has 1000 turns. Find secondary turns and ratio I_s/I_p if primary draws 1 A.
example.solution: N_s / N_p = V_s / V_p, so N_s = N_p × (V_s / V_p) = 1000 × (12/230) ≈ 52 turns. Power: P = V_p I_p = 230 × 1 = 230 W. Secondary current: I_s = P / V_s = 230 / 12 ≈ 19.2 A. Ratio I_s / I_p ≈ 19.2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Transformers use mutual inductance to trade voltage for current (or vice versa) without losing power. Essential for transmitting electricity long distances.

image.alt: Transformers — Electromagnetic Induction

slides.title: Solved Problem: Eddy Current Braking

example.problem: A copper disk (radius r = 0.1 m, thickness t = 0.01 m) rotates in a perpendicular magnetic field B = 0.5 T. At rotation rate ω = 100 rad/s, estimate the retarding torque due to eddy currents. (Resistivity ρ = 1.7 × 10^-8 Ω·m.)
example.solution: Eddy currents are induced in the disk as it cuts field lines. Motional EMF between center and rim ε ≈ (1/2) B ω r^2 ≈ 0.5 × 100 × (0.1)^2 / 2 ≈ 0.25 V. Equivalent resistance of current path R ≈ ρ L / A, where L ~ r and A ~ t × r. R ≈ (1.7 × 10^-8) × 0.1 / (0.01 × 0.1) ≈ 1.7 × 10^-7 Ω. Current I ≈ ε/R ≈ 0.25 / (1.7 × 10^-7) ≈ 1.5 × 10^6 A (huge due to low R; rough estimate). Retarding torque τ ≈ B I r^2 — for more precision, solve curl equations, but the key is τ ∝ B^2 ω.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eddy currents in conductors moving through magnetic fields create drag (retarding torque). This is how magnetic brakes work in trains and elevators.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Eddy Current Braking — Electromagnetic Induction

points.text: A power plant generates 10 kW at 100 V. This must be transmitted 1 km through copper wire (resistance 0.1 Ω per 100 m, so total R = 1 Ω). Compare power loss in two scenarios: (a) direct transmission at 100 V; (b) step-up to 10 kV, transmit, then step-down to 100 V. Assume ideal transformers.

example.problem: Calculate power loss in each case.
example.solution: (a) Direct at 100 V: I = P/V = 10000/100 = 100 A. Power loss P_loss = I^2 R = (100)^2 × 1 = 10,000 W = 10 kW (entire power lost!). (b) Step up to 10 kV: Primary I_p = 100 A; secondary I_s = (V_p/V_s) × I_p = (100/10000) × 100 = 1 A. Line loss P_loss = (1)^2 × 1 = 1 W (negligible). After step-down at receiver, power is 10 kW at 100 V. Higher voltage transmission dramatically reduces losses.

image.alt: Challenge: Power Transmission Loss — Electromagnetic Induction

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Magnetic flux Φ = B A cos(θ); measured in webers (Wb).
Faraday's law: induced EMF ε = −dΦ/dt. Lenz's law: induced current opposes the change causing it.
Motional EMF: ε = BLv for rod moving perpendicular to B; ε = NBA ω sin(ωt) for rotating coil.
Self-inductance L and mutual inductance M govern back-EMF when current changes.
Transformers: voltage and current scale inversely (V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p). Step-up reduces current, reducing transmission loss.
Eddy currents in moving conductors create drag; used in brakes and power-factor correction.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electromagnetic induction converts motion and changing flux into electricity. Transformers leverage it to move power across the grid efficiently—that's why we have AC power worldwide.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Electromagnetic Induction

subject: Physics
title: AC Power in Your Home
hook: Your ceiling fan runs on AC current that reverses 50 times per second. Anjali discovers how RMS voltage, impedance, and resonance govern the devices in her home.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student measuring voltage and current in AC circuits

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Tutor explaining phasors, impedance, and power factor

slides.title: Alternating Current
slides.storyContext: Anjali's home runs on 50 Hz AC current. But what does that mean? Ravi shows her with an oscilloscope: 'The voltage sine wave reverses 50 times per second.'

image.alt: Alternating Current — Alternating Current

slides.title: AC in Every Outlet
slides.storyContext: Anjali plugs her phone charger into an outlet in Delhi and wonders: why AC, not DC like a battery? Ravi explains: 'AC (alternating current) at 230 V, 50 Hz comes from India's power grid. Generators make AC by rotating coils in magnetic fields—it's natural. AC is easy to step up and down with transformers, so we can transmit power across the country without huge losses. Your charger converts it to DC inside.'

image.alt: AC in Every Outlet — Alternating Current

slides.title: AC Voltage and Current

points.label: Sinusoidal form
points.text: AC voltage V(t) = V₀ sin(ωt + φ), where V₀ is peak voltage (amplitude), ω = 2πf is angular frequency, f is frequency (Hz), φ is phase (rad). In India: f = 50 Hz, ω = 100π rad/s, effective voltage V_rms = 230 V.

points.label: RMS (root-mean-square) value
points.text: For sinusoidal signal: V_rms = V₀ / √2 ≈ 0.707 V₀. Similarly I_rms = I₀ / √2. Home meters display RMS values. 230 V (RMS) corresponds to peak V₀ = 230√2 ≈ 325 V.

points.label: Average power
points.text: Average power P = V_rms I_rms cos(φ), where φ is phase difference between voltage and current. Coefficient cos(φ) is power factor (PF).

image.alt: AC Voltage and Current — Alternating Current

slides.inSimpleWords: AC voltage and current oscillate sinusoidally. The 230 V displayed on a meter is the RMS value (effective value), not peak. Peak is 325 V.

slides.title: AC in Resistive, Inductive, and Capacitive Circuits

points.label: Resistor (R)
points.text: V and I are in phase (phase difference 0°). Impedance Z_R = R. Current I = V/R.

points.label: Inductor (L)
points.text: Voltage leads current by 90° (V ahead of I in phase). Inductive reactance X_L = ωL = 2πfL (ohms). Impedance Z_L = jωL (j = imaginary unit). Current I = V / X_L lags voltage.

points.label: Capacitor (C)
points.text: Current leads voltage by 90° (I ahead of V). Capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(ωC). Impedance Z_C = −j/(ωC). Current I = V × ωC leads voltage.

image.alt: AC in Resistive, Inductive, and Capacitive Circuits — Alternating Current

slides.inSimpleWords: Resistors let current flow freely. Inductors resist current changes (oppose it). Capacitors block DC but let AC pass, leading in phase.

slides.title: RLC Series Circuit and Impedance

points.label: Total impedance
points.text: For R, L, C in series: Z = √[R² + (X_L − X_C)²] = √[R² + (ωL − 1/(ωC))²] (ohms). Phase angle φ: tan(φ) = (X_L − X_C) / R.

points.label: Current
points.text: I = V / Z = V / √[R² + (ωL − 1/(ωC))²]. Current lags voltage if X_L > X_C (inductive); leads if X_C > X_L (capacitive); in phase if X_L = X_C (resonance).

points.label: Resonance
points.text: At resonance frequency ω₀ = 1/√(LC), reactances cancel: X_L = X_C. Impedance Z = R (minimum), current is maximum I_max = V/R, and V and I are in phase (φ = 0, PF = 1).

example.problem: An RLC circuit has R = 100 Ω, L = 0.5 H, C = 100 μF, and is driven at f = 50 Hz. Find Z and phase angle φ.

slides.inSimpleWords: AC circuits combine resistance (friction), inductance (inertia of magnetic field), and capacitance (elastic charge storage). At resonance, they work most efficiently.

image.alt: RLC Series Circuit and Impedance — Alternating Current

slides.title: Power Factor and Real vs Reactive Power

points.label: Real power (P)
points.text: Power actually consumed (converted to heat, work): P = V_rms I_rms cos(φ) = I_rms² R (watts, W). Only resistive component dissipates energy.

points.label: Reactive power (Q)
points.text: Power oscillating between source and L or C: Q = V_rms I_rms sin(φ) = I_rms² X (volt-amperes reactive, VAR). No net energy transfer.

points.label: Apparent power (S)
points.text: S = V_rms I_rms = √(P² + Q²) (volt-amperes, VA). Power factor PF = cos(φ) = P/S. Ideal PF = 1 (pure R); lagging PF (inductive); leading PF (capacitive).

image.alt: Power Factor and Real vs Reactive Power — Alternating Current

slides.inSimpleWords: Real power (P) is what you pay for—energy used. Reactive power (Q) is energy sloshing back and forth in inductors/capacitors. Power factor tells you how much of the current is actually doing work.

slides.title: AC Generators and Transformers (Revisited for AC)

points.label: Generator EMF
points.text: Rotating coil: ε(t) = ε₀ sin(ωt), where ε₀ = NBA ω = NBA × 2πf. For India: ε_rms = 230 V at 50 Hz.

points.label: Transformer equation (AC)
points.text: V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p (voltage ratio), I_s / I_p = N_p / N_s (current ratio inverse). Power conserved: V_p I_p cos(φ_p) = V_s I_s cos(φ_s) (assuming ideal transformer).

points.label: Transmission lines
points.text: Power P = V I cos(φ). For fixed P, higher V means lower I, reducing resistive loss I² R. Transformers step up (13 kV → 400 kV) at power plant, step down at substation.

slides.inSimpleWords: AC generators output sinusoidal voltage naturally. Transformers scale voltage and current for efficient transmission and safe home use.

image.alt: AC Generators and Transformers (Revisited for AC) — Alternating Current

slides.title: Solved Problem: Induction Motor Startup

example.problem: An induction motor (modeled as R + X_L in series) draws 230 V at 50 Hz. Motor specs: R = 10 Ω, L = 0.5 H. Find startup current and power factor.
example.solution: X_L = ωL = 100π × 0.5 ≈ 157 Ω. Z = √(10² + 157²) ≈ 157.3 Ω. Startup current I = 230 / 157.3 ≈ 1.46 A. Power factor cos(φ) = R/Z = 10/157.3 ≈ 0.064 (very low—mostly reactive). Real power P = I² R = (1.46)² × 10 ≈ 21.4 W; reactive power Q ≈ I² X_L ≈ 335 VAR. As motor speeds up, inductance effect reduces, PF improves.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inductive loads (motors, fluorescent lights) lag—current lags voltage. This wastes reactive power and reduces efficiency until the motor reaches steady speed.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Induction Motor Startup — Alternating Current

points.text: A factory has an inductive load drawing 100 kW at power factor PF = 0.8 (lagging). Electricity costs Rs. 8 per kVA-month (apparent power), and the tariff penalties low PF. To improve PF to 0.95, what capacitance should be added in parallel?

example.problem: Calculate required capacitance at 50 Hz, assuming V_rms = 400 V.
example.solution: Real power P = 100 kW (fixed). Initial: P = S cos(φ), so S_initial = 100/0.8 = 125 kVA. Reactive power Q_i = S √(1 − cos²(φ)) = 125 × √(1 − 0.64) ≈ 75 kVAR. Target PF = 0.95: S_target = 100/0.95 ≈ 105.3 kVA. Final reactive power Q_f = 105.3 × √(1 − 0.95²) ≈ 33 kVAR. Required capacitor: Q_C = Q_i − Q_f = 75 − 33 = 42 kVAR. Capacitive reactance X_C = V²/Q_C = (400)² / (42 × 10³) ≈ 3.8 Ω. Capacitance C = 1/(ωX_C) = 1/(100π × 3.8) ≈ 840 μF.

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: AC voltage V(t) = V₀ sin(ωt). RMS value V_rms = V₀/√2 for sinusoids.
Impedance Z combines resistance, inductive reactance X_L = ωL, and capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(ωC).
In RLC circuits, resonance occurs at ω₀ = 1/√(LC), where Z = R (minimum) and PF = 1.
Real power P = V_rms I_rms cos(φ) is work done; reactive power Q oscillates. Power factor PF = cos(φ) measures efficiency.
Transformers step voltage up/down for efficient power transmission and safe home supply.
AC power reaches every home, driving lights, fans, refrigerators, and motors. Efficient transmission (high V, low I) requires transformers.

slides.inSimpleWords: AC power oscillates 50 times per second in India. RLC circuits respond differently at different frequencies; resonance maximizes power transfer. Transformers enable long-distance transmission.
